title: Fed's Williams Expects Inflation to Ease but Warns Rate Hikes Remain on the Table
excerpt: The New York Fed president said disinflationary forces should reassert themselves, but the central bank stands ready to raise borrowing costs if price pressures persist above the 2% target.
body:
• New York Fed President John Williams told Reuters he expects inflation to decline in the second half of 2026 and into 2027, targeting 2% by 2028
  • Williams warned the Fed would "absolutely" raise rates if inflation fails to fall back toward its target
  • Three FOMC members dissented at last week's meeting, calling for immediate rate increases to combat inflation stuck above 2% for over five years
  • The Fed held rates steady at 3.50%–3.75%, with Williams saying he "strongly supported" the decision

New York Federal Reserve President John Williams said he remains optimistic that inflation will gradually cool, but made clear the central bank is prepared to raise interest rates if price pressures do not subside — a signal that the Fed is far from declaring victory on its most stubborn economic challenge.

In an interview with Reuters on Friday, Williams said the main drivers that pushed inflation higher over the past 18 months — trade tariffs, energy price spikes, and surging demand from artificial intelligence investment — may be losing steam.

"I think that some of the big drivers that pushed up inflation will not be at play as much, and then some of the disinflationary forces that we've been seeing should reassert themselves."

— John Williams, President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York

Holding Steady Amid Dissent

The comments came days after the Federal Open Market Committee voted to keep the federal funds rate unchanged at 3.50%–3.75%, a range where it has sat since December 2025. Williams said he "strongly supported" that decision.

But the hold was not unanimous. Three Fed officials dissented, each arguing in statements released Friday that the central bank needs to raise borrowing costs to bring inflation down. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack was among them.

"Inflation has remained stubbornly above 2% for more than five years, and I am not confident it will return to our objective on its own," Hammack said.

The Fed's preferred inflation gauge — the personal consumption expenditures price index — rose 3.7% year-over-year in June, nearly double the central bank's 2% target. Earlier in July, Williams described inflation as "unquestionably too high at about 4%."

A Conditional Outlook

Williams's optimism is hedged with conditions. He said his personal forecast calls for inflation to decline in the second half of 2026 and fall further in 2027, with the 2% target achievable on a sustained basis by 2028. In a July 15 speech, he projected inflation reaching approximately 3.25% by year-end.

But he was unequivocal about the alternative scenario. "If the economy is not on a trajectory that will bring inflation back down to 2%, it would absolutely be appropriate to act to get us on a trajectory that does bring inflation back to 2%," Williams said.

Financial markets have already begun pricing in a decent chance of a rate hike by year end. Long-term bond yields have been climbing as investors worry that inflation will remain elevated. Futures traders see the FOMC as roughly split between those who see no need for a hike and those who expect at least one 25-basis-point increase this year.

Middle East and Energy Uncertainty

The wildcard in the inflation outlook remains energy prices. The Middle East conflict has repeatedly disrupted oil markets, and Williams acknowledged "ample uncertainty" around when energy costs might ease. He said a resolution of hostilities and the resumption of shipping traffic could bring swift improvement, but that the situation "could change depending on circumstances."

In early July, Williams expressed optimism that oil prices had peaked, but renewed hostilities have since pushed energy costs higher again.

New Fed Communications Era

Williams's willingness to lay out a conditional framework stands in contrast to the approach of new Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, who has moved away from providing forward guidance about the policy outlook. Williams said the Fed would not feel bound by market expectations in setting policy.

"We always have to come do our own analysis, do our hard work, assess all of the factors influencing the economy, the outlook," he said.

What It Means for Indian Americans

For the Indian diaspora in the United States, the Fed's path carries direct consequences. Persistent inflation above 3.5% continues to erode purchasing power on everything from groceries to housing. The interest rate outlook also affects the dollar-rupee exchange rate — a key factor for the millions who send remittances to India annually. A rate hike would likely strengthen the dollar further, making remittances more valuable in rupee terms but also reflecting tighter financial conditions in the U.S. Meanwhile, India's Reserve Bank has been charting its own course on rates, and any Fed tightening would widen the policy divergence between the two central banks.

Williams also offered a reassuring note on the AI sector, saying recent volatility in tech valuations is not surprising and that leverage levels among AI-focused firms are not a financial stability concern. "Most of these businesses have very high earnings, so I'm not as worried about the financial stability from the leverage right now," he said — a point relevant to the large Indian-American workforce in the technology industry.
nri_angle: Persistent US inflation and potential rate hikes affect Indian-American purchasing power, dollar-rupee remittance values, and the large diaspora workforce in AI and tech sectors.
